reason: Could not break it, with one weakness noted and repaired. The verifier took wording from Bartlett, which by rule 2 is a fame signal and not a verification; on its own that would not pass. I therefore checked a Pope edition directly: the Wikisource transcription of The Works of Alexander Pope (1717), Essay on Criticism, reads 'True ease in writing comes from art, not chance, / As those move easiest who have learn'd to dance.' with the full stop after 'dance' and 'learn'd' elided, exactly the wording proposed, followed by ''Tis not enough no harshness gives offence'. Gutenberg 7409 (school edition) agrees on words, modernises to 'learned' and drops the stop, and its marginal [361] on the preceding line confirms the couplet is lines 362 to 363. Part II runs 201 to 559, and Bartlett's 'Part ii, line 162' is 362 overall, so the locator is right. The couplet is a complete sentence. Pope reused it in altered form in the Imitations of Horace, Epistle II.ii ('But ease in writing flows from art, not chance'), which is a different line and does not disturb this citation. Source leads with the name, no dash, about 70 characters; '(1711)' is the first publication year, acceptable though the lower-case nouns are those of the collected Works rather than the 1711 quarto. shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Pope yearCount 0, not banned. Poetry is the form. On theme exactly: the writers on the work of writing.
betterCitation: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism, Part II, lines 362 to 363 (1711; text of the Works, 1717)
